subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Afternoon Tea Invented
description: A 60-second lesson on Afternoon Tea Invented.

hook.text: In the 1840s, Anna Russell, Duchess of Bedford, felt a 'sinking feeling' every afternoon around four.

buildup.text: Dinner wasn't until eight. She asked servants to bring tea, bread, butter, and cakes to her room.

discovery.text: She began inviting friends. The informal gathering became fashionable among London's upper class.

twist.text: Afternoon tea and high tea are different. High tea is a working-class meal; afternoon tea is delicate snacks.

climax.text: Hotels like the Ritz and Claridge's turned afternoon tea into a grand event that tourists still flock to.

punchline.text: One duchess got hungry. A global tradition was born.

quiz.question: Who is credited with inventing afternoon tea?

details.summary: Anna, the Duchess of Bedford, is credited with inventing afternoon tea around 1840 to bridge the long gap between lunch and late dinner. She began requesting tea, sandwiches, and cakes in the afternoon and invited friends to join. The practice quickly became a fashionable British social ritual.
details.whyItMatters: Afternoon tea created one of the world's most enduring social rituals. It structured the British day and became a global symbol of refined hospitality.
takeaways: The Duchess of Bedford invented afternoon tea around 1840
It bridged the gap between lunch and late dinner service
The practice became a fashionable social ritual across Britain

faq.question: What is the difference between afternoon tea and high tea?
faq.answer: Afternoon tea is a light, elegant affair served on low tables with finger sandwiches, scones, and pastries around 4 PM. High tea is a more substantial working-class meal served at the dining table around 5 to 6 PM with hearty foods. The terms are often confused but describe very different occasions.

faq.question: Is afternoon tea still popular in Britain today?
faq.answer: Yes, though more as a special occasion than a daily habit. Hotels and tea rooms across Britain serve formal afternoon tea. It has become a popular tourist experience and celebratory treat. The tradition has also been exported to former British colonies and beyond.
